variants.title: Count the acknowledgements
variants.context: For one replica set, W + R > RF guarantees every successful write acknowledgement set and read response set share a replica. QUORUM needs a majority: floor(RF ÷ 2) + 1 responses.
variants.prompt: A keyspace has replication factor 3. How many replica responses does a QUORUM write need before the coordinator replies?
variants.hint: A quorum is a majority of the replica set.
variants.explanation: floor(3 ÷ 2) + 1 = 2. QUORUM writes plus QUORUM reads overlap because 2 + 2 > 3.

mistakes.feedback: Three would be ALL. A quorum is a majority, and one replica can be down.
One response is level ONE; it does not guarantee overlap with a QUORUM read.

variants.title: Count the acknowledgements
variants.context: For one replica set, W + R > RF guarantees every successful write acknowledgement set and read response set share a replica. QUORUM needs a majority: floor(RF ÷ 2) + 1 responses.
variants.prompt: A keyspace has replication factor 5. How many responses does QUORUM need?
variants.explanation: floor(5 ÷ 2) + 1 = 3. Two replicas can be unavailable and a QUORUM operation still succeeds.

mistakes.feedback: Two of five is not a majority; two QUORUM sets could miss each other.
Five is ALL. Any single failure would block the operation.

variants.title: Count the acknowledgements
variants.context: For one replica set, W + R > RF guarantees every successful write acknowledgement set and read response set share a replica. QUORUM needs a majority: floor(RF ÷ 2) + 1 responses.
variants.prompt: Replication factor is 3 and writes use consistency ONE. What is the smallest read consistency, in responses, that guarantees a read set overlaps every successful write set?
variants.explanation: 1 + R > 3 means R = 3, which is ALL. Cheap writes push the cost onto reads, and any replica outage then blocks the read.

mistakes.feedback: 1 + 2 = 3 does not exceed 3; a QUORUM read could miss the single replica that acknowledged.
1 + 1 = 2 is far below the replication factor.

variants.title: Fix the partition
variants.context: The partition key is hashed to a token and decides placement. Clustering columns order rows inside one partition; they do not redistribute a hot partition. Replication copies a partition; it does not split it.
variants.prompt: One tenant’s partition takes most of the cluster’s writes. Will raising the replication factor from 3 to 5 help?
options: Yes. More replicas share the write load.
Yes, if reads switch to LOCAL_ONE.
No. Every copy receives the same writes.
optionFeedback: Every replica of the partition applies every write to it.
Read levels change read cost; the write hot spot is unchanged.
Replication adds redundancy and work per write; it cannot shard one logical partition.
variants.hint: What does each replica of a hot partition receive?
variants.explanation: Replication cannot rescue a hot partition. Add a bucket such as a day or hash suffix to the partition key so the tenant spreads across owners.

variants.title: Fix the partition
variants.context: The partition key is hashed to a token and decides placement. Clustering columns order rows inside one partition; they do not redistribute a hot partition. Replication copies a partition; it does not split it.
variants.prompt: A device-telemetry partition keyed by device_id grows without bound. Which change bounds its size without changing the query for one device?
options: Add a time bucket, such as (device_id, day).
Add event_time as another clustering column.
optionFeedback: More copies of an unbounded partition make the problem larger.
A composite key with a daily bucket caps each partition and keeps single-device reads direct.
Clustering columns order rows inside the partition; they do not bound its growth.
variants.hint: Which part of the primary key decides placement and size?
variants.explanation: Only the partition key changes placement and bounds the unit. A time bucket keeps each partition small while the caller still names device and day.

variants.title: Fix the partition
variants.context: The partition key is hashed to a token and decides placement. Clustering columns order rows inside one partition; they do not redistribute a hot partition. Replication copies a partition; it does not split it.
variants.prompt: Product wants “find all devices that reported a status for a tenant today,” but the table is keyed by (device_id, day). What is the Cassandra-shaped answer?
options: Add a secondary index and scan every device partition.
Use ALLOW FILTERING on the production table.
Write a second table keyed for that query.
optionFeedback: Scanning many partitions is exactly what the data model is supposed to avoid.
Filtering across partitions is table-wide work dressed as a query.
Each important query gets its own projection with a direct key path.
variants.hint: Every table is a query-specific projection.
variants.explanation: Cassandra moves design into the schema: one business fact may live in several tables so each query names a bounded partition.

variants.title: Route a write
variants.context: Cassandra hashes the partition key to a token, finds the token owners on the ring, applies the keyspace replication strategy and rack topology, then the coordinator waits for the consistency level’s acknowledgements.
variants.prompt: A client sends a mutation to any node. Put the coordinator’s steps in order.

items.text: Apply the keyspace replication strategy and rack topology to pick replicas.
Locate the token range and its owners on the ring.
Hash the complete partition key to one token.
Send to the replicas and wait for the consistency level’s acknowledgements.

variants.hint: Placement happens before any replica is contacted.
variants.explanation: Hash → owners → replicas by policy → acknowledgements. NetworkTopologyStrategy spreads replicas across the racks and datacenters the snitch reports.

variants.title: Route a write
variants.context: Cassandra hashes the partition key to a token, finds the token owners on the ring, applies the keyspace replication strategy and rack topology, then the coordinator waits for the consistency level’s acknowledgements.
variants.prompt: A token-aware driver sends a write. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Choose replicas per datacenter using the configured replication factor.
Compute the token from the partition key so the driver can pick a likely replica.
Return to the client only when the chosen consistency level is satisfied or a timeout fires.
Find the ring range containing that token.

variants.hint: A token-aware driver still follows the same ownership steps.
variants.explanation: The driver only shortens the first hop. Ownership, replica choice, and the acknowledgement wait are unchanged.

variants.title: Route a write
variants.context: Cassandra hashes the partition key to a token, finds the token owners on the ring, applies the keyspace replication strategy and rack topology, then the coordinator waits for the consistency level’s acknowledgements.
variants.prompt: A write times out. Reconstruct what happened, in order.

items.text: The coordinator failed to collect enough acknowledgements in time and reported a timeout.
The mutation was sent to all configured replicas.
The key was hashed and the token owners were found.
Replicas were chosen according to the keyspace policy.

variants.hint: A timeout is about acknowledgements, not about whether the mutation was sent.
variants.explanation: The mutation may have been applied by some replicas. A timeout means “not enough acknowledgements”, so retries must be idempotent.

variants.title: Converge after failure
variants.context: There is no permanent leader. Hints replay missed writes on a best-effort basis; repair compares replicas with Merkle trees and streams differences; tombstones must not be purged before stale replicas are repaired.
variants.prompt: A replica was down for ten minutes and is back. What guarantees it catches up?
options: Repair; hints are best effort and may not cover everything.
Hints alone; they always replay every missed write.
Nothing is needed; QUORUM reads fix replicas automatically.
optionFeedback: Repair compares replicas and streams differences; it is the durable convergence path.
Hints shorten common outages but can be dropped or expire.
Read repair can help individual keys that happen to be read; it is not systematic.
variants.hint: Which mechanism is designed to be complete rather than fast?
variants.explanation: Hints are a best-effort handoff. Scheduled repair is what makes replicas converge, and its I/O belongs in capacity planning.

variants.title: Converge after failure
variants.context: There is no permanent leader. Hints replay missed writes on a best-effort basis; repair compares replicas with Merkle trees and streams differences; tombstones must not be purged before stale replicas are repaired.
variants.prompt: An operator purges tombstones older than a few hours to save space. Later, deleted rows return. Why?
options: A stale replica still held the live value.
Tombstones cannot be removed in Cassandra.
optionFeedback: Purging a tombstone before every replica has seen it lets an old live value win later.
Tombstones are removed after gc_grace_seconds and successful repair.
Reads do not create data; a stale replica does.
variants.hint: What does a tombstone need to outlive?
variants.explanation: A delete is a timestamped tombstone. Purge it before stale replicas are repaired and deleted data can reappear.

variants.title: Converge after failure
variants.context: There is no permanent leader. Hints replay missed writes on a best-effort basis; repair compares replicas with Merkle trees and streams differences; tombstones must not be purged before stale replicas are repaired.
variants.prompt: A write timed out. The client retries. What must be true of the operation?
options: The retry must go to a different datacenter.
The retry must use a lower consistency level.
optionFeedback: Location does not remove the possibility of a duplicate apply.
A timeout means the coordinator lacked acknowledgements, not that nothing was written.
Lowering the level changes the contract; it does not make a duplicate write safe.
variants.hint: What does a write timeout actually tell you?
variants.explanation: “Not enough acknowledgements in time” is ambiguous. Retries are safe only when applying the mutation twice is harmless.
